statement: The supplied source [wikipedia:Likelihood_function] genuinely contains nothing to derive, as it contains no derivation of the log-likelihood function (such as converting a product of independent likelihoods to a sum via log_of_product_to_sum). Instead, the source provides definitions and properties of the likelihood function: for a continuous random variable X with density f_θ(x), the likelihood is defined as L(θ | x) = f_θ(x); for a discrete random variable, L(θ | x) = p_θ(x) = Pr{X = x | Θ = θ}; or more generally, any function of θ equal to c * Pr[x | θ] for some positive constant c. The logarithm of the density, log f(x | θ), is evaluated under regularity conditions for parameter estimation.

symbols.meaning: deterministic but unknown model parameter or parameter vector
observed outcome of the random variable X
random variable representing the observed data
likelihood function of θ given observation x
probability density function of continuous random variable X at outcome x given parameter θ
probability mass function of discrete random variable X at outcome x given parameter θ
Hessian matrix of second partial derivatives of the likelihood function with respect to parameter components
gradient vector of partial derivatives of the likelihood function with respect to parameter components
parameter space, an open connected subset of ℝ^k

properties.property: Maximizing the probability density at observation x_j is equivalent to maximizing the likelihood of the specific observation: argmax_θ L(θ | x_j) = argmax_θ f(x_j | θ).
properties.why: the ratio of the interval likelihood over [x_j, x_j + h] to h converges to the density f(x_j | θ) as h -> 0+ by the first fundamental theorem of calculus

properties.property: The likelihood function L(θ | x) is not a probability density or probability mass function over θ, and its integral or sum over the parameter space need not equal one.
properties.why: it is a function of the parameter θ given an observed outcome x rather than a probability distribution over θ

properties.property: For an observation from a discrete component of a mixed distribution with discrete probability mass p_k(θ), the likelihood is L(θ | x) = p_k(θ).
properties.why: maximizing the probability mass at x amounts to maximizing the likelihood of the specific discrete observation

properties.property: Under regularity conditions for parameter estimation, the partial derivatives ∂ log f / ∂θ_r, ∂² log f / ∂θ_r ∂θ_s, and ∂³ log f / ∂θ_r ∂θ_s ∂θ_t exist for all r, s, t = 1, ..., k for almost all x and all θ ∈ Θ.
properties.why: they ensure the existence of a Taylor expansion of the log-density around the parameter vector

properties.property: There exists a unique maximum likelihood estimator θ̂ ∈ Θ if L(θ) is twice continuously differentiable on open connected Θ ⊆ ℝ^k, the Hessian H(θ) = [∂²L / ∂θ_i ∂θ_j] is negative definite at every θ where ∇L vanishes, and lim_{θ -> ∂Θ} L(θ) = 0.
properties.why: negative definiteness of the Hessian at all stationary points ensures uniqueness of the interior maximum under vanishing boundary conditions

assumptions.assumption: The random variable X follows an absolutely continuous distribution with density f_θ(x) or a discrete distribution with probability mass p_θ(x).
assumptions.breaks_when: The probability distribution cannot be dominated by Lebesgue measure or counting measure (e.g., singular distributions lacking a Radon-Nikodym derivative with respect to a common dominating measure).

assumptions.assumption: The parameter space Θ is an open connected subset of ℝ^k and the likelihood function is twice continuously differentiable on Θ.
assumptions.breaks_when: The parameter space is discrete, has boundaries where the maximum occurs, or the likelihood function is non-differentiable.

assumptions.assumption: For repeated coin flip or sample trials, observations are assumed to be independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.).
assumptions.breaks_when: Trials exhibit serial dependence, non-stationarity, or varying parameters across observations.

assumptions.assumption: Partial derivatives of the density f with respect to θ up to third order are bounded in absolute value by integrable functions F_r(x), F_rs(x), and H_rst(x).
assumptions.breaks_when: The support of the density f(x | θ) depends on the parameter θ or the density lacks integrable dominating bounds.

failure_modes.mode: Confusing likelihood with posterior probability P(θ | x)
failure_modes.signature: Treating L(θ | x) as a probability distribution over θ that can be integrated or summed to 1.
failure_modes.cause: Failing to apply Bayes' theorem; L(θ | x) evaluates data probability given θ, not parameter probability given data.

failure_modes.mode: Non-existence or non-uniqueness of the maximum likelihood estimate
failure_modes.signature: The gradient ∇L has no vanishing point, multiple vanishing points, or the Hessian H(θ) fails to be negative definite.
failure_modes.cause: Non-concavity of the likelihood, non-compact parameter space without boundary vanishing, or stationary points being saddle points or local minima.

failure_modes.mode: Incomparability of likelihoods across different statistical models
failure_modes.signature: Likelihood comparisons or likelihood ratios produce invalid or scale-dependent conclusions.
failure_modes.cause: Likelihoods are constructed from Radon-Nikodym derivatives with respect to different, non-commensurate dominating measures.

failure_modes.mode: Breakdown of Taylor expansion regularity conditions
failure_modes.signature: Asymptotic normality or consistency of maximum likelihood estimators cannot be established.
failure_modes.cause: The derivatives of log f fail to exist up to third order or exceed integrable dominating bounds.

canon_notes: canon expects a derivation but no source performs one, so log_likelihood is recorded as a definition
